screenings.title: Germany, Year Zero
screenings.description: GERMANIA, ANNO ZERO Italy/France/Germany, 1948 Directed by Roberto Rossellini Starring Edmund Moeschke, Ernst Pittschau, Ingetraud Hinze Approx. 78 min. 35mm. Following the international acclaim and box office success of ROME, OPEN CITY and PAISAN, Rossellini took the first of many obstreperous swerves that would come to define his career. His next film would be another dispatch from war-torn Europe, with scenes playing out amidst the rubble with unvarnished immediacy, with unfamiliar and nonprofessional actors populating the cast—but this time, the protagonists would not be resistance fighters liberating Italy, but the defeated Germans muddling through their wasteland reich. Financed largely by the French government, GERMANY, YEAR ZERO became an experiment in radical empathy and its limits, casting about for signs of new life in a nation of crooks, unrepentant Nazis, and pederasts. The only innocent soul is twelve-year-old protagonist Edmund, who cannot qualify for a work permit, but must somehow earn a living to support his household. Even the child recognizes that he has no role models in this world: his brother is a mopey ex-soldier who refuses to register for a ration card, his father is an invalid who muses he’d be better off dead, his neighbors are coarse and severe, his friends are common swindlers, and his former school teacher still preaches that the strong must snuff out the weak. Unsentimental in the extreme and devoid of any comic relief, GERMANY YEAR ZERO plays like a seance for souls who have yet to recognize themselves as the walking dead. 35mm print courtesy Cinecittà.

screenings.title: The Housemaid
screenings.description: Cited by Bong Joon-ho as an inspiration on his Parasite and widely regarded by South Korean cinephiles and scholars as one of the country’s greatest films, The Housemaid can now be discovered by the rest of the world thanks to a restoration by the Korean Film Archive and Martin Scorsese’s World Cinema Project. The routine domestic life of a middle-class family is turned upside-down after a young woman (Lee Eun-shim) joins the household to help with the chores—though what she does instead is turn the house into a boiling cauldron of lust. A mélange of melodrama, morality tale, noir thriller, and horror film that, in Kim’s handling, come together to exercise a vice-like grip.

screenings.title: Basic Instinct
screenings.description: The brainchild of provocateur extraordinaires Paul Verhoeven and Joe Eszterhas, Basic Instinct was one of the most controversial films of the 90s (protested by LGBTQ activists for its portrayal of the film’s bisexual femme fatale) and a runaway box office smash. When detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas) becomes ensnared in a web of sex, lies, and violence, all the evidence points to Catherine Tramell (Sharon Stone, in a star-making role), a seductive, mysterious crime novelist. As the bodies pile up and hidden obsessions are revealed, Curran begins to doubt his investigatory instincts and give in to his baser ones.

screenings.title: Fatherland
screenings.description: ★★★★★ “Another expansive, enriching work from a modern master.” – Phil de Semlyen, Time Out “A perfectly cut jewel of a movie... The power of the movie creeps up on you with its emotional restraint, the beauty of its black-and-white images and the delicacy with which Pawlikowski explores the devastations trembling under the faces of both father and daughter...” – Manohla Dargis, The New York Times “Stunning... an exquisite study of family, identity, and art where future ideals are intertwined with historical remorse.” – Tomris Laffly, Elle “[A] damn-near perfect period piece... Told with exacting restraint yet as layered as the lacquer on an ebony Biedermeier console, this forms a loose triptych with Pawlikowski’s last two features, IDA and COLD WAR, both of which were set at least partly behind the Iron Curtain... It is immaculately performed by Zischler and especially Hüller, grounding the film throughout with an uncanny, expressive stillness. But it is also exquisitely rendered in the same boxy ratio and silvery monochrome lensing Pawlikowski and DP Lukasz Zal (THE ZONE OF INTEREST) deployed on IDA and COLD WAR, and scrupulously detailed down to the ruined buildings, sharply cut suits, surly restaurant service and eclectic selection of jazz, classical and folk tunes chosen by Pawlikowski, all of which is sure to set discriminating viewers swooning.” – Leslie Felperin, The Hollywood Reporter

screenings.title: Flight to Hell
screenings.description: A garish amalgam of Westworld and The Mummy, Passeri’s 2000 masterpiece addresses the controversial practice of planting microchips in mummies in order to staff fantasy theme parks. Transcending its influences, the film boasts a uniquely queasy visual style crafted from greasy animatronics and a painfully saturated color palette. The plot concerns two dimwitted American journalists caught in the meltdown of the titular Mummy Theme Park – this, of course, is of secondary significance beside the exercise in discount worldmaking achieved through Passeri’s fabric-store scenography and a script rife with non-sequiturs.

screenings.title: Raise the Red Lantern
screenings.description: China/Hong Kong, 1991 Directed by Zhang Yimou Starring Gong Li, Saifei He, Jingwu Ma, Cuifen Cao In Mandarin with English subtitles Approx. 125 min. Nineteen-year-old Songlian, a promising student whose family has been destroyed by her father’s death, is forced to abandon her studies and marry into wealth, becoming the fourth and newest concubine of the aging, unseen Master Chen. Inside his walled estate, she discovers a household ruled by a merciless ritual: each night, red lanterns are lit outside the chambers of whichever wife the master chooses to visit, granting her privilege and status while the others are cast into cold irrelevance. Songlian is drawn into the orbit of her rivals, each shaped by years of fighting for the same scraps of attention. Determined at first to rise above the games, Songlian is gradually worn down by isolation and humiliation until she strikes back, trading secrets and favors to secure her place in Master Chen’s hierarchy. As petty cruelty turns even more dire, Songlian is forced to confront what these desperate measures will cost her soul. Newly restored, RAISE THE RED LANTERN remains a landmark of Fifth Generation Chinese cinema and 1990s international film. The 4K restoration of RAISE THE RED LANTERN was carried out by the Udine Far East Film Festival on the occasion of its 26th edition. The original image and sound negatives were used under the supervision of Director Zhang Yimou. The vintage positive copy, presented at the 1991 Venice International Film Festival and preserved at the Venice Biennale's Historical Archive of Contemporary Arts, was used for color reference. The restoration was made in 2024 at L'Immagine Ritrovata (Hong Kong – Bologna). Presented with support from The Reginald S. Reinhardt, Ling-Makekau Fund for Asia-Pacific Films and The Ada Katz Fund for Literature in Film A FILM MOVEMENT RELEASE

screenings.description: The little-screened debut feature by Yang, prophet of and proselytizer for the Taiwanese New Wave, features Sylvia Chang and Terry Hu as two female friends, an unhappily married housewife and a concert pianist, brought together after a 13-year separation: their process of catching up illustrated through an innovative, ingeniously layered flashback structure which shows the director’s air for formal experimentation already fully in operation. Shot by renegade cinematographer Christopher Doyle, also on his first feature, Yang’s gorgeous and deeply felt memory piece/mystery uses its intricate structure to explore, among other things, “the ways in which patriarchal authority stunts young people’s lives.” US theatrical premiere of new 2K restoration.

screenings.description: An infamous triple filicide has escaped from Ashecliffe Hospital, located on a rugged islet in Boston Harbor that bears a striking resemblance to Arnold Böcklin’s Island of the Dead, and US Marshal Chuck Aule and his new partner (Leonardo DiCaprio and Mark Ruffalo) are on the scene to investigate. Set in the postwar period that gave birth to some of the most anguished of all film noir, Scorsese’s feverish thriller is awash in the psychic trauma of the mid-century, its soundtrack a catalog of jarring modernist classical compiled by collaborator Robbie Robertson and including work by Krzysztof Penderecki, John Cage, and Max Richter, among others, with Robert Richardson’s cinematography suggesting a particularly jaundiced, blighted version of the Technicolor process.

screenings.title: Little Fugitive
screenings.description: U.S., 1953 Directed by Morris Engel, Ruth Orkin, Ray Ashley Co-written and Co-produced by Ray Ashley Starring Richie Andrusco WINNER Venice Film Festival – Silver Lion, 1953 NOMINEE Academy Awards® – Best Writing, 1954 Approx. 75 min. Brooklynite Richie Andrusco’s on the run from the cops after the accidental shooting of his big brother—only trouble is, Richie’s only seven, the “shooting” was just a dumb ketchup-splashed gag by his brothers and cronies, and Mom won’t be back from Grandma’s till the next day. But with six bucks in his pocket and all of Coney Island for a hide-out, how tough can things be, as Richie rides the merry-go-round, takes a cowboy photo, tries out his swings in the batting cage, scarfs down hot dogs, soda, watermelon, and corn on the cob, and gets hooked on the pony ride—he refinances by scouring under the boardwalk for two-cent deposit soda bottles—and even his frantically searching big brother takes a break to ride The Parachute Jump. With a concealed custom-made 35mm camera (which Godard later asked to borrow), legendary photographer Engel—and crew including future wife Ruth Orkin, herself a photography titan—captured unknowing crowds, a phenomenal performance by pint-sized non-pro Richie, and a perfect time capsule of Coney in the waning years of its heyday. Presented with support from The Robert Jolin Osborne Endowed Fund for American Classic Cinema of the 1930s, ’40s, and ’50s

Featuring animation supremely attentive to the syntax of kitty motion and the vocal talents of Eva Gabor and Scatman Crothers who gets to lead on the boppin' classic “Everybody Wants to Be a Cat.”

Wall-to-wall with elaborate, antic gags, though also marked by a quiet sense of pastoral beauty that had previously been given little outlet.

screenings.title: The Muppet Christmas Carol: The Uncut Version
screenings.description: Dir. Brian Henson. 1992, 85 mins. U.S. DCP. With Michael Caine, Dave Goelz, Steve Whitmire, Jerry Nelson, Frank Oz. In this beloved staple of many a childhood, the Charles Dickens classic is recast with the classic Muppet characters, including Gonzo as Charles Dickens, Kermit at Bob Cratchit, and Fozzie Bear as Fozziwig. This faithful adaptation is as full of Christmas spirit and imagination as any of the various film adaptations of the novel, and features a towering performance by Caine as the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge and a splendid musical score by Paul Williams. This full, uncut version of the original release features the song “When Love Is Gone.” Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. screenings.title: The Sacrifice
screenings.description: Made when Tarkovsky was already suffering greatly from the lung cancer that would end his life, his last film is one of cinema’s greatest final testaments, a work that puts both pagan and Christian traditions of self-sacrifice into dialectic conversation. Shot in Sweden with renowned cinematographer Sven Nykvist and featuring several other Ingmar Bergman collaborators, including actor Erland Josephson, the gorgeous and deeply affecting film, winner of the Grand Prix at Cannes, takes place at a birthday gathering that’s interrupted by news warning of an imminent nuclear holocaust.

screenings.title: Secrets & Lies
screenings.description: The winner of the Palme d’Or at the 1996 Cannes Film Festival, Leigh’s tender, funny, fearless film has Brenda Blethyn in a career-best performance as Cynthia, a white working-class woman who has a life-changing revelation when she meets Black middle-class optometrist Marianne Jean-Baptiste, who informs Cynthia she’s the little girl Cynthia had given up for adoption 27 years ago, all grown up. Developed, like all of Leigh’s films, through a process of collaborative improvisation, it’s a film of startling spontaneity and uncomfortable, unflinching emotional honesty.

screenings.title: Bells Are Ringing
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1960, 126 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Judy Holliday, Dean Martin, Fred Clark, Jean Stapleton. In his delightful musical pairing with Oscar-winner Judy Holliday and superstar Dean Martin, Minnelli directs an effervescent New York–set romantic comedy about a nosy Brooklyn telephone operator for an answering service who finds herself falling for a poor wannabe playwright while also trying to play matchmaker to her other clients. With her tender, metropolitan vivaciousness, Holliday is as note-perfect as always, while the film is also a showcase for the musical talents of composers Betty Comden and Adolph Green, from whose Broadway hit the show is adapted. Bells Are Ringing would be the final musical from the famed MGM Freed Unit, and earned Minnelli a DGA nomination for Best Director. Four people give different accounts of a man’s murder and the rape of his wife, which Kurosawa presents with striking imagery (those shafts of sunlight streaming through the forest canopy!) and ingenious use of flashbacks. Shooting the celebrated opening of his film—a torrential downfall at Rashomon Gate—Kurosawa and crew mixed water with black ink in the rain tank, creating one of the most sinister soaks in cinema history.

screenings.title: Medea (1988)
screenings.description: Based on an unfilmed screenplay by Carl Theodor Dreyer and, of course, Euripides’s tragedy of the same title, von Trier’s made-for-television film—save for two epiphanic eruptions—is uncharacteristically austere, the enfant terrible of Danish cinema making himself a medium for the Old Master’s vision, setting the source material in a pre-Christian Denmark. “An experimental film in the true sense of the word… Taking the greatest limitation of video—the medium’s lack of depth of field—Mr. von Trier turns it into a strength, flattening perspectives in a way that collapses his foreground characters into the tumultuous backgrounds (waves, wind-swept fields) that surround and dominate them.” —Dave Kehr, The New York Times

screenings.title: Mean Streets
screenings.description: In New York City’s Little Italy, a devoutly Catholic mobster must reconcile his desire for power, his feelings for his epileptic girlfriend, and his devotion to his troublesome friend.

screenings.title: Columbus
screenings.description: Modern architecture acts as a vehicle for emotional expression in Kogonada’s lauded first feature, whose title refers to the Indiana city that, thanks to the patronage of Cummins diesel engines company cofounder J. Irwin Miller, has commissioned buildings from master builders including I.M. Pei, Eero Saarinen, and Robert Venturi. A Korean American translator (John Cho) arrives in this curious testing ground for advanced architecture after his estranged scholar father falls ill, there to cross paths with dad’s protégée (Parker Posey), an aesthete clerk at the local library (Haley Lu Richardson), and a bevy of singular structures. A film of rich colors and muted yearning, and one of the most distinctive debuts in the last decade of American independent cinema.

screenings.title: The Best Secret Agent
screenings.description: The movie that lit the fuse on an explosion of espionage thrillers in Taiwan, Zhang’s box-office phenomenon is a twisty tale of star-crossed love and sabotage during the years of the Sino-Japanese war, featuring Bai Hong as a refugee from the marauding Japanese who land in Shanghai, Ke Junxiong as the man she falls for, and Tian Qing as the collaborationist stooge of the puppet Manchukuo state that she reluctantly marries—his schemes constantly undermined by the actions of a mysterious “Secret Agent Heaven No. 1.” A spry, stylish, sexy cloak-and-dagger melodrama, based on a homonymous 1945 film from the Mainland, with Hong a delight as she dons several walk-in closets’ worth of disguises.

screenings.title: Compartment No. 6

When Damiel falls in love with lonely trapeze artist Marion, the angel longs to experience life in the physical world. Featuring a showstopping performance by a young Nick Cave, crooning the title track from From Her to Eternity, Wings of Desire is one of the most inexhaustible modern films.

screenings.description: Wendy Carlos’s score of switched-on Moog synthesizer classical, Kubrick’s punchy framings, and Malcolm McDowell’s cruelly charismatic, Nadsat slang-spouting performance as teen reprobate Alex combine to make for cracking cinema, and a hallucinatory imagination of a future broken Britain. Based on the stinging satire by Anthony Burgess, a work by turns exhilarating and nauseating, the film of A Clockwork Orange would be withdrawn from British cinemas at Kubrick’s behest, citing concern over reports that it had inspired copycat crimes in the UK.

screenings.title: A Separation
screenings.description: Farhadi combines elements of the domestic drama and psychological thriller in his trenchant, lacerating 2012 Academy Award winner for Best Foreign Film. Simin (Leila Hatami) wants to emigrate with her 11-year-old daughter and with or without her husband, Nader (Payman Maadi), who, with the support of the court, has dug in his heels to keep the family in place while he looks after his ailing father, aided by a caregiver with costly secrets. Through the intersecting stories of two deadlocked couples—one middle-class, the other working-class—and their necessary deceptions, Farhadi shows us a microcosm of contemporary Iranian society and the insoluble moral dilemmas it presents to ordinary men and women.

screenings.title: You Can See Everything
screenings.description: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.

screenings.title: Father of the Bride
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1950, 92 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Spencer Tracy, Elizabeth Taylor, Joan Bennett, Don Taylor, Billie Burke. Forty years before it was remade into another beloved comedy starring Steve Martin and Diane Keaton, Minnelli’s sparkling original Father of the Bride delighted audiences with its perfect mix of caustic comedy and sentiment. A superb Spencer Tracy stars as strait-laced businessman Stanley Banks, whose life unravels when the apple of his eye (a teenage Elizabeth Taylor) announces she’s getting married. With its pointed satire of perfect postwar suburbia and clever portrait of a well-intentioned but disgruntled family man sent to the edge of sanity by the trappings—and out-of-control cost—of putting on a good(bye) show for his daughter, the Best Picture–nominated Father of the Bride kicked off the 1950s in smart, funny style and remains a treasure of its era. screenings.description: Inspired by the writings of legendary hobo Leon Ray Livingston, under the pen name “A-No.1,” Aldrich’s tale of the risks run rail-riding in the ’30s northwest stars Lee Marvin as top tramp A-No.1, locked in a battle royale struggle with Ernest Borgnine’s fascistic, hobo-hatin’ conductor Shack on the speeding #19 of the Oregon, Pacific and Eastern Railroad, while Keith Carradine’s rascally fellow stowaway looks on. Featuring gorgeous location photography, suicidal stuntwork on speeding period locomotives, and bone-breaking action, Emperor of the North is Aldrich at his brutal best.

Minnelli’s breathtaking Best Picture winner stars the ever-captivating Gene Kelly as a painter struggling to make ends meet in the city of light on the G.I. Bill, torn between his adoration of a beautiful dancer (Leslie Caron) and his pragmatic need for the attention of an elegant arts patron (Nina Foch). With a thrilling, all-Gershwin score and a spectacularly designed, climactic dream ballet sequence shot by the brilliant cinematographer John Alton, An American in Paris is pure cinematic bliss and a musical movie landmark filled with such Gershwin gems as “I Got Rhythm,” “’S Wonderful,” “Our Love Is Here to Stay” and “I’ll Build a Stairway to Paradise.” Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. Screens with A Child Already Knows, in which Sia, employing Mao-era kid’s cartoons and other archival morsels, recounts her family’s flight from Shanghai to Hong Kong.

screenings.title: The Manchurian Candidate
screenings.description: The 1960 U-2 incident, and rumors of the brainwashing of downed Air Force pilot Francis Gary Powers by Soviet captors, were fresh in the imagination when Frankenheimer’s taut political suspenser hit screens, featuring Laurence Harvey as Raymond Shaw, a Korean War vet returned stateside with decorations after going MIA—unbeknownst to himself and the wider world, a sleeper agent programmed to do the bidding of the Commies—and Frank Sinatra the Army Intelligence officer who suspects all might not be right with Sgt. Shaw. “One of the strangest and most mercurial movies ever made in Hollywood… Conceivably the only commercial American film that deserves to be linked with the French New Wave, full of visual and verbal wit that recalls Orson Welles… A powerful experience, alternately corrosive with dark parodic humor, suspenseful, moving, and terrifying.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, The Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Basic Instinct
screenings.description: The brainchild of provocateur extraordinaires Paul Verhoeven and Joe Eszterhas, Basic Instinct was one of the most controversial films of the 90s (protested by LGBTQ activists for its portrayal of the film’s bisexual femme fatale) and a runaway box office smash. When detective Nick Curran (Michael Douglas) becomes ensnared in a web of sex, lies, and violence, all the evidence points to Catherine Tramell (Sharon Stone, in a star-making role), a seductive, mysterious crime novelist. As the bodies pile up and hidden obsessions are revealed, Curran begins to doubt his investigatory instincts and give in to his baser ones.

screenings.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.title: Six Suspects
screenings.description: Keeping an eye on his ex-lover (Zhang Qingqing), the personal assistant to the chairman of a large steel company, private eye Kong-hui (Wu Dongru) picks up ample fodder to blackmail the folks in the front office—and so, when Kong-hui is found murdered, detective Yi Yuan won’t lack for suspects… though each trail he follows seems to lead to a dead end. A jazzy, ingeniously plotted urban whodunnit set in a Taipei in the first flush of postwar prosperity, Six Suspects was not granted a theatrical release on completion but has now been revealed, thanks to restoration work by the Taiwan Film Institute, as a darkly glittering gem of the mid-century Taiyupian.

screenings.title: Millennium Mambo
screenings.description: A stylish and seductive submersion into the techno-scored neon nightlife of Taipei, Hou’s much-misunderstood marvel stars Shu Qi (The Assassin) as an aimless bar hostess drifting away from her blowhard boyfriend and towards Jack Kao’s suave, sensitive gangster. Structured as a flashback to the then-present from the then-future of 2011, it’s a transfixing trance-out of a movie, drenched in club lights, ecstatic endorphin-rush exhilaration, and a nagging undercurrent of ennui. Hou and longtime cinematographer Lee here break from their familiar pattern of elegantly composed long shot long takes to create something both more intimate and hectic, a film whose shallow-focus images, jittery camerawork, and cramped locations evoke both the claustrophobic character of Taiwan’s capital city and, in Lee’s words, “the feeling of youth.”

screenings.title: The Ascent
screenings.description: The bloodthirsty and seemingly unstoppable Nazi war machine is on the march towards Moscow in Shepitko’s wrenching, snow-swept World War II drama, which begins with two Soviet peasant soldiers foraging for food in a Belarusian village and proceeds to tell an emotional, lyrical tale of loyalty and betrayal, partisanship and collaboration, and, ultimately, the possibility of transcendent redemption. Shepitko’s final feature, frequently cited as among the greatest of Soviet films, won the Golden Bear at the 1977 Berlin Film Festival, just two years before its director’s tragic death in a car accident at age 41.

screenings.title: The Rescuers
screenings.description: Geraldine Page, Bob Newhart, and Eva Gabor are among the vocal talent assembled for Disney’s vivacious adaptation of Margery Sharp’s beloved book series about the Rescue Aid Society, a group of dauntless mice who travel the world to lend aid to kidnapping victims. Here R.A.S. representatives Miss Bianca (Gabor) and Bernard (Newhart) rush to Devil’s Bayou, Louisiana, where they liberate a little girl named Penny from the clutches of the nefarious Madame Medusa (Page) and her trained crocodiles, Brutus and Nero, while at the same time tasked with keeping a precious gemstone safe from the villainess. A spirited, swashbuckling adventure, made with brio by Disney’s crack animation team led by rising star Don Bluth.

screenings.title: A Boy Named Charlie Brown
screenings.description: Dir. Bill Melendez. 1969, 85 mins. U.S. 35mm. The beautifully animated A Boy Named Charlie Brown was the first theatrical Peanuts feature, and it remains the best. Directed by Disney and Looney Tunes animation veteran Bill Melendez, whom cartoonist Charles M. Schulz had first entrusted with bringing his characters to life on the groundbreaking television specials A Charlie Brown Christmas and It’s the Great Pumpkin, Charlie Brown, this gentle musical comedy follows our eternally disappointed “blockhead” as he navigates baseball losses, kite-eating trees, and his own anxieties while preparing to compete in the National Spelling Bee championship in New York. Linus and Lucy, Schroeder and Snoopy—the whole gang—is here, as is the great Vince Guaraldi, supplying a jazzy, Oscar-nominated score, plus a musical centerpiece dream sequence set to Beethoven’s Sonata Pathétique, which expands the animated world of the Peanuts into uncharted realms of visual experimentation. screenings.description: The 1960 U-2 incident, and rumors of the brainwashing of downed Air Force pilot Francis Gary Powers by Soviet captors, were fresh in the imagination when Frankenheimer’s taut political suspenser hit screens, featuring Laurence Harvey as Raymond Shaw, a Korean War vet returned stateside with decorations after going MIA—unbeknownst to himself and the wider world, a sleeper agent programmed to do the bidding of the Commies—and Frank Sinatra the Army Intelligence officer who suspects all might not be right with Sgt. Shaw. “One of the strangest and most mercurial movies ever made in Hollywood… Conceivably the only commercial American film that deserves to be linked with the French New Wave, full of visual and verbal wit that recalls Orson Welles… A powerful experience, alternately corrosive with dark parodic humor, suspenseful, moving, and terrifying.” —Jonathan Rosenbaum, The Chicago Reader

screenings.title: Brigadoon
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1954, 108 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Gene Kelly, Cyd Charisse, Van Johnson, Elaine Stewart. One of the first Cinemascope, Technicolor musicals, this MGM extravaganza, adapted from the stage by the great Lerner and Loewe, is an enchanting fantasy in which a pair of New Yorkers find themselves in a magical Scottish town called Brigadoon, which only materializes once every hundred years. No inhabitant of the town can cross the border to leave, or else the town will disappear—but a stranger can stay if he falls in love with someone there. Of course, complications ensue when Gene Kelly’s Tommy finds himself pining for the beautiful Fiona (Cyd Charisse). Featuring splendidly beautiful dance sequences and gorgeous set design, Brigadoon is a poignant supernatural romance about the aching ephemerality of existence. screenings.title: Barbara Forever + Q&A
screenings.description: BARBARA FOREVER is an expansive, immersive exploration of the life, work, and ongoing cultural impact of filmmaker Barbara Hammer – a pioneering artist who lived boldly, created urgently, and transformed cinema through her singular vision. Her films were an extension of herself: sensual, experimental, and unapologetically lesbian, rooted in a profound desire for connection and an insistence on telling her own story. Driven by her canon of over eighty films, a vast collection of unreleased archival materials, and extensive audio interviews, Brydie O’Connor’s portrait allows for Hammer’s voice and images to shine through, becoming both a tribute and an extension of her legacy.

screenings.title: Dragon Superman
screenings.description: A breakout success that spawned two sequels in rapid succession, Dragon Superman introduced Taiwanese audiences to the titular masked crusader, by day straight-arrow newspaperman San Lin, by night the bane of the chaos-sowing, satin suit-clad, hydrocephalic members of the Cosmos Gang. Fans of the Adam West Batman series, Mario Bava’s Danger: Diabolik, Japanese tokusatsu pictures, and swinging ’60s superheroics in general will find much to enjoy in this vivacious action romp, starring Kuei Chih-pang as the be-scarfed, motorcycle-riding vigilante, who has his hands full protecting a blind chanteuse (Wu Min), a supermarket magnate (Yang Weixi), and a hunk of Incan gold from the ne’er-do-wells.

screenings.title: Arthur
screenings.description: Dir. Steve Gordon. 1981, 97 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Dudley Moore, Liza Minnelli, John Gielgud, Geraldine Fitzgerald, Jill Eikenberry. This madcap New York City farce stars Dudley Moore as an alcoholic playboy man-child who has lived off the millions inherited from his parents and has never had to work a day in his life. Aided in all endeavors public and private by his endlessly sharp-tongued butler Hobson (an Oscar-winning John Gielgud, delivering one incredible one-liner after another), Arthur lives in a cocoon of privilege, until he falls hard for Liza Minnelli’s down-to-earth working-class shoplifter Linda Marolla. What Arthur lacks in sensitivity towards its character’s drinking problem, it more than makes up for in its perfect mix of sweetness and laugh-out-loud hilarity, and Moore and Minnelli make one of the 1980s’ greatest and most unexpected romcom couples. screenings.title: The Piano
screenings.description: Gale-force winds and interminable lashing rain render colonial New Zealand a nigh uninhabitable mire in Campion’s elemental Antipodean Gothic romance, in which mute Scotswoman Ada and her young daughter (Holly Hunter, Anna Paquin) arrive under the Southern Cross so that Ada can be wed to stiff-backed settler Alisdair Stewart (Sam Neill)—an arranged union that quickly sours when Stewart separates Ada from her lone means of expression, her piano, and Ada drifts into an increasingly compromising and sexualized relationship with neighbor George Baines (Harvey Keitel), an ex-sailor and the instrument’s new owner. With its Palme d’Or win at Cannes, Campion became the first female director to receive that honor—and a shower of Academy Awards still lay ahead.

screenings.title: Gremlins
screenings.description: Dir. Joe Dante. 1984, 106 mins. DCP. With Zach Galligan, Phoebe Cates, Hoyt Axton, Frances Lee McCain. This dark comic gem, directed by Joe Dante and produced by Steven Spielberg, is a cheerfully nasty throwback to fifties B-monster-movies in which a Rockwell-ready American town falls under siege at Yuletide to a horde of mischievous, murderous beasts. With its gruesome kitchen set piece (in which a lovable mom slices, dices, and microwaves a handful of the creatures) and unforgettably grim Phoebe Cates monologue about why she hates Christmas, Gremlins might not be for young children, but its subversive exuberance can make an adult feel like a kid again. Featuring wildly convincing practical puppet and stop-motion effects, which run the gamut from adorable to nightmarish, Gremlins helped ensure the invention of the MPAA’s PG-13 rating. screenings.title: Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.description: Sofia works as a location scout for a TV pilot filming in New York City. It’s her job to find the homes, businesses, and exteriors where the show will be filmed. Driving around the city’s different neighborhoods, she enters the private spaces of strangers to photograph their cozy apartments and eclectic shops, stepping into the fabric of their lives while trying to satisfy the demands of her erratic employers. Over a day filled with these encounters, Sofia witnesses moments of curiosity, vulnerability, and quiet tension until her work takes a sudden, personal turn. Drawing from her own experience as a location scout, writer-director Paula González-Nasser captures the poetry and costs of being a young creative. Her celebrated directorial debut The Scout crafts a contemplative exploration of urban disconnection, following one woman’s journey through other people’s worlds as she struggles to find her own.

screenings.title: Tokyo Sonata
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s reputation was made as perhaps the most formidable figure in the “J-horror” boom, so his about-face into contemporary-set shomin-geki melodrama à la Yasujirō Ozu was an unexpected—but not unwelcome—surprise… though beneath the placid surface of Tokyo Sonata, sinister stirrings are very much visible. Salaryman Teruyuki Kagawa, newly out of work, struggles to keep up the illusion of employment for his family, consisting of one son who lights out to join the US Army, another with a not-so-dirty secret of his own (the scamp is taking piano lessons), and a wife (Kyōko Koizumi) who finds an unlikely solution to her unhappy domestic existence when she’s kidnapped by a home invader. Winner of the Prix Un Certain Regard at the 61st Cannes Film Festival.

screenings.title: Keane
screenings.description: Kerrigan, whose debut Clean, Shaven was one of the most harrowingly immersive portrayals of schizophrenia ever put on screen, dove back into the depths of a turbulent, fractured mind with the equally-if-not-more accomplished Keane, in which Damian Lewis, playing a mentally unsound William Keane, wanders the dingy corridors of the Port Authority Bus Terminal and other sordid pockets of New York City. Haunted by the memory of his young daughter’s abduction, he eventually strikes up a relationship with a young mother and her child (Amy Ryan and Abigail Breslin). A work of brilliantly sustained discomfort and tactile seediness, raw, rigorous, and entirely riveting.

screenings.title: New Yorkers + Before the First Word
New York, New York
screenings.description: Dir. Martin Scorsese. 1977, 164 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Robert De Niro, Liza Minnelli, Lionel Stander. Scorsese’s ode to classic MGM musicals and 1940s jazz marked a departure for him, combining his gritty hard-boiled realism (he had just made Taxi Driver) with a celebration of the surreal artificiality of Hollywood. Undoubtedly one of the director’s masterworks, the film brilliantly depicts the difficulty of a marriage between two independent creatives, and Scorsese pushes the story of the doomed relationship between a jazz singer and a saxophonist into dark, exhilarating territory. The final half hour, when Scorsese gives the film over to pure movie musical magic, makes for one of his most sustained feats of grand filmmaking, while Minnelli’s climactic belting of the now-classic title song (written by Fred Ebb and John Kander for the film) is a true showstopper. screenings.title: Jane Elliott Against the World
screenings.description: The morning after Martin Luther King Jr.’s assassination, Jane Elliott divided her all-white third-grade class in Riceville, Iowa, by eye color. Her lesson in discrimination made her a national figure and a target. Nearly sixty years later, Jane Elliott Against the World finds her as funny and combative as ever. She stands with students, teachers, and families in Temecula, California, fighting restrictions on teaching race and history. At home, her daughters ask her to acknowledge what her refusal to stay silent has cost them. The woman who spent a lifetime asking others to change must now try to change herself.

screenings.title: Angel Guts: Red Classroom
screenings.description: Overwrought with an exuding sense of melancholia in tone and exuberant mise-en-scène, Chusei Sone’s adroitly self-reflexive Red Classroom is a brooding, almost lyrical portrait of Takashi Ishii’s tragic figures of Muraki and Nami, buried in relentless traumas, desires and deep loneliness.

screenings.title: Drinking and Driving
screenings.description: Early twenties Iris (Jillian Frank) and Palmer (Avalon Fast) never left their hometown. They work at the same restaurant, share the same bed, and both have a habit of drinking and driving. They run into Levi (Ethan Hawksworth), a guy they used to know. They spend time with him and his cousin, Phoenix (Henri Gillespi), in cars, backyards, and other people’s bedrooms. When Levi shares a dream he had with Iris, things change between the four of them. The reality of the summer becomes faded, the parties die. The four end in a field of unified confusion.

screenings.title: Michael Mann's Manhunter: The Final Cut
screenings.description: The film that introduced audiences to psychiatrist-cum-serial killer Hannibal Lecter—here spelled “Lecktor,” the role originated by a wonderfully gelid Brian Cox—Mann’s magnificent thriller stars William Petersen as Will Graham, an FBI profiler whose day-and-night dedication to his work threatens to unravel his psyche, recruiting Dr. Lecktor to help him track down an at-large murderer whose penchant for masticating his prey has led police to dub him the Tooth Fairy. (The part is played by a looming, melancholy Tom Noonan.) Mann, whose “MTV cops” series Miami Vice was a primetime giant when Manhunter was released, recognized the crucial importance of a good soundtrack, and this one’s a doozy, with tracks from Shriekback, The Reds, and The Prime Movers, and Iron Butterfly’s “In-A-Gadda-Da-Vida” providing a needle drop for the ages.

screenings.title: It Follows
screenings.description: Mitchell’s Detroit-shot sophomore film, winner of the Next Wave award at Austin’s Fantastic Fest in 2014 and the breakout horror phenomenon of the following year, is a work of potent sexual dread, in which erotic congress transmits something much worse than a dose of clap: the attentions of a spectral, shape-shifting entity that pursues the afflicted with methodical single-mindedness, a pursuit that ends in terrible carnage. Enigmatic and unsettling, its thick atmosphere of paranoia incalculably added to by a soundtrack courtesy electronic musician Disasterpiece (Rich Vreeland), per Pitchfork “a score that announces when something is about to happen, only to suddenly upend expectations and leave the room on edge.”

screenings.title: Kaili Blues
screenings.description: Chinese filmmaker Bi Gan’s award-winning directorial debut is an audacious work that announced a major new filmmaking talent. Country doctor Chen Sheng sets out on a train journey to search for his brother’s abandoned child, only to find himself in a dreamlike world where the boundaries between past, present, and future—and between fantasy and reality—are porous. This remarkable visual achievement, which feels as singular and alien as the films of Apichatpong Weerasethakul, was shot in the mining village Kaili, the director’s birthplace, and incorporates poetry he’s been writing since he was a teenager.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. Distributor: Grasshopper Film

screenings.title: The Band Wagon
screenings.description: Dir. Vincente Minnelli. 1953, 111 mins. U.S. 35mm. With Fred Astaire, Cyd Charisse, Oscar Levant, Nanette Fabray, Jack Buchanan. One of the crowning glories of American musical cinema, Minnelli’s The Band Wagon is a triumph of the form, recycling the old backstage theater formula into a winsomely graceful celebration of the virtues of popular art. Playing a version of himself as an aging Hollywood star, Astaire leads a cast that includes Fabray and Levant, standing in for the film’s real-life writers Betty Comden and Adolph Green; Buchanan, incarnating a pretentious, blowhard actor-director à la Orson Welles; and Charisse, playing the ballet dancer turned show business ingénue she then was. The Band Wagon elevates these Hollywood traditions to new heights of technical display (“A Shine on Your Shoes”), self-reflexive comedy (“That’s Entertainment!”), and sublime visual poetry (“Dancing in the Dark”). Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Peggy
screenings.description: Dir. Charles Giblyn, Thomas H. Ince. 1916, 70 mins. U.S. Restored DCP courtesy of the Academy Film Archive. With Billie Burke, William Desmond, William H. Thompson, Charles Ray. Though most of the films featuring silent cinema star Billie Burke (the future Glinda the Good Witch in The Wizard of Oz) have been lost, Peggy was restored by the Academy Film Archive in 2018. Starring Burke as an independent-minded, wealthy young woman from New York who causes a stir when she moves to a remote village in Scotland, Peggy captures Burke’s dynamism, joie de vivre, and comedic brilliance. Burke was also well known as a fashion plate, and this film showcases the actress in her trend-setting one-piece “Billie Burke” pajamas, as well as an array of beautiful clothing provided by some of the most renowned couture designers of the period, including Lucile, Lady Duff Gordon. This screening is presented in conjunction with Bard Graduate Center Gallery’s exhibition Goddesses in the Machine: Fashion in American Silent Film (on view now until January 3, 2027), which features a short excerpt from the film. This screening offers the rare opportunity to see the film in its entirety, and it will be introduced by Goddesses in the Machine co-curators Michelle Finamore and Emma Cormack. Herald for Peggy, 1916. Gift of William R. Bogert, Jr. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: The Saga of Anatahan
screenings.description: Visionary Josef von Sternberg had once been a feared and revered presence on the Paramount Studios lot, but after one too many clashes over his obsessive perfectionism rendered him all but unemployable, and a falling out with Howard Hughes over his Jet Pilot, “Jo” went independent, directing, writing, shooting, and narrating this sublimely artificial picture, shot entirely on a Kyoto soundstage, about a dozen Japanese seamen stranded on a Pacific Island with one woman—unaware that World War II has long since ended, and that a little war of their own is in the making. A favorite film of one of von Sternberg’s students during his tenure teaching at UCLA, none other than Mr. Mojo Rising himself, Jim Morrison.

screenings.title: Blue + Chinese Series
screenings.description: Over the same, unceasing monochromatic sea of blue, Yves Klein’s patented “International Klein Blue,” the voices of Jarman and collaborating actors (including Tilda Swinton and Nigel Terry) read a poetic text by the director in which he muses on the physical and mental deterioration wrought by the ravages of AIDS, as well as the endless implications of the color blue. Jarman would be gone within a year, but he left behind one of the great final films, a vibrant work of courage and clarity in the face of oblivion. Screens with Brakhage’s Chinese Series, a long-contemplated short work inspired by Chinese ideograms completed in the filmmaker’s dying days.

screenings.title: 67 Bombs to Enid + Q&A
screenings.description: Between 1946 and 1958, the U.S. detonated 67 nuclear bombs in the Marshall Islands, contaminating the region and leaving generations of Marshallese facing illness. Decades later, many of the survivors and their descendants are building a new life in the United States.

screenings.title: The Inugami Family
screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Time Indefinite
screenings.description: His complicated relationship with his aging surgeon father, his settling into married life and fatherhood in early middle-age—these subjects, the sort of foundational building blocks of life so central as to often be taken for granted, are at the center of McElwee’s autobiographical documentary Time Indefinite, a film that brings a dry, laconic humor to its very serious meditations on mortality, family, and spirituality. “A rich and compelling cinematic experience… Conveys a sensuous appreciation of the physical world that is so acute that the environment is almost as important as the people… Communicates a sense of the elusive moment in all its complexity and richness being captured.” —The New York Times

screenings.title: Top Stripper
screenings.description: Directed with remarkable levity, and vibrant, on-location cinematography, Morita’s Top Stripper is an irreverent take on the seishun eiga, raising questions of spectatorship as a young boy falls in love with a dancer. Treating sex as a mere fact of life, Morita captures his subjects' personal lives with heartfelt candor.

screenings.title: You Can See Everything
screenings.description: Thirty-four days before she’s sent to prison, notorious Silicon Valley founder Elizabeth Holmes invites a skeptical film crew to document her every move. What begins as an intimate portrait of an enigmatic felon becomes a mind-bending three-year journey into the abyss.

screenings.title: Rains Over Babel (Llueve sobre Babel)
screenings.description: Dir. Gala del Sol, Colombia/U.S./Spain, 2025, 111 min. In Spanish with English subtitles. A retro-futuristic, queer tropical-punk riff on Dante’s Inferno, Rains Over Babel follows a band of misfits converging at Babel, a dive bar that doubles as purgatory and is presided over by La Flaca—the city’s Grim Reaper. Here, souls gamble years of their lives in hopes of outwitting Death Herself. Among them are Dante, racing to uncover his past; Monet, a ghost desperate to reclaim his body; Timbí and Uma, descending through hell to save their loved ones; and Jacob, preparing for his first drag performance. Acclaimed at the Sundance Film Festival, this love letter to Cali, reimagined as the mythical City of Maya, fuses magical and gritty realism into a vibrant, psychedelic universe of love, identity, gender fluidity, resilience, and second chances. Colombia’s official submission for Best International Feature at the 99th Academy Awards. New York Premiere Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: ACE Presents: Day Night Day Night
screenings.description: Before her epic My Undesirable Friends made Loktev one of the most-discussed figures in contemporary nonfiction, there was Day Night Day Night, the director’s riveting fiction feature debut, closely following 48 hours in the life of an unnamed young woman, played by an entrancing Luisa Colón, as she makes preparations to detonate herself in a Times Square suicide bombing in service to an unknown cause. Shot with remarkable immediacy and adroitness by cinematographer Benoît Debie, best known for his collaborations with Gaspar Noé, and lent a sense of subtly rising tension that reaches a point of near-suffocation by editor Michael Taylor, Loktev’s austere film—and its brooding, taciturn leading lady—exert a sinister undertow pull of fascination.

screenings.title: Full Metal Jacket
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1987. 116 mins. 35mm. With Matthew Modine, Adam Baldwin, Vincent D’Onofrio, R. Lee Ermey, Dorian Harewood, Arliss Howard, Kevyn Major Howard, Ed O’Ross. Wearing a peace symbol and a helmet marked “Born to Kill,” Joker (Modine) is a military journalist trying to maintain his cynicism and sanity during basic training and combat in Kubrick’s harrowing Vietnam drama. Unlike concurrent films about the U.S. involvement in the war in Southeast Asia, such as Platoon, Kubrick’s film is by design unemotional, taking as its main subject the dehumanization of the American war machine itself, personified in the first half by the abusive drill sergeant played by R. Lee Ermey and in the second by the mechanical, distanced nature of the violent battles themselves. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Woman on the Night Train
screenings.description: New English Subtitles by Japan Society. A baroque fantasy by way of Vadim and Buñuel’s Diary of a Chambermaid, Noboru Tanaka’s Woman on the Night Train is a gothic work replete with decadent, atmospheric imagery and unravelling psyches.

screenings.title: Remake
screenings.description: Setting out to document the process of turning his 1985 nonfiction classic Sherman’s March into a fiction film—while reeling from the death of his 27-year-old son, Adrian—McElwee, in his first film following a 14-year hiatus, gives an enormously tender cinematic eulogy that is also something of a summation of his filmmaking life, describing among many things the tenuous tightrope walk between necessary consideration of practical, commercial concerns and a relentless striving towards honesty and integrity. All of the elements that constitute McElwee’s peculiar genius—the diarist’s warts-and-all self-revelation, the paring away of inessentials in pursuit of universal truths, the off-kilter comic vision—are to be found in spades in the many layers that comprise the extraordinary Remake.

screenings.title: Scent of a Spell
screenings.description: 2K Restoration. Mermaid Legend director Toshiharu Ikeda’s elegant and spellbinding Scent of a Spell is a moody, psychological tale of a “woman in trouble”, melding eroticism, tragic coincidence and psychological paranoia.

screenings.title: Tokyo Sonata
screenings.description: Kurosawa’s reputation was made as perhaps the most formidable figure in the “J-horror” boom, so his about-face into contemporary-set shomin-geki melodrama à la Yasujirō Ozu was an unexpected—but not unwelcome—surprise… though beneath the placid surface of Tokyo Sonata, sinister stirrings are very much visible. Salaryman Teruyuki Kagawa, newly out of work, struggles to keep up the illusion of employment for his family, consisting of one son who lights out to join the US Army, another with a not-so-dirty secret of his own (the scamp is taking piano lessons), and a wife (Kyōko Koizumi) who finds an unlikely solution to her unhappy domestic existence when she’s kidnapped by a home invader. Winner of the Prix Un Certain Regard at the 61st Cannes Film Festival.

screenings.title: Taxi Driver
screenings.description: “Suck on this!” A pure distillation of needling isolation, inadequacy, and anguish, all roiling in the tortured gut of Robert De Niro’s insomniac cabbie Travis Bickle, who cruises all night through a stygian, steam-choked Manhattan, nursing his fears and hatreds. A defining picture of New York City in 1976, and a movie that is wrenched straight from the unquiet psyche of its screenwriter, exorcizing his personal demons.

screenings.title: What Is the City but the People?
Salò, or the 120 Days of Sodom
screenings.description: Pasolini’s final film remains one of the most shocking ever made. Set during a waning fascist Italy’s dark days amidst World War II, Salò updates the writings of Marquis de Sade to create a repugnant tale of four wealthy libertines who kidnap a group of teenage boys and girls and enact horrific humiliations and violence upon them. A formally and conceptually brilliant, if relentlessly nauseating, portrayal of man’s most debased instincts and the capitalist systems that allow them to thrive. Per Pasolini, “The most sincere thing I could do at that moment was to make a film about a mode of sexuality whose joyousness is a compensation for repression—a phenomenon that was about to come to an end, forever.”

screenings.title: Wallace & Gromit: The Classic Shorts
screenings.description: Along with the Academy Award–winning success of Aardman Animations’ 1990 Creature Comforts, it was this trio of inspired shorts featuring cheese-loving, jug-eared, Wigan-based crackpot inventor Wallace and his erudite pet dog/straight man/frequent savior Gromit that established the company as a stop-motion dynasty to delight all ages. Featuring A Grand Day Out, in which Wallace whips up a homemade spaceship in order to sample lunar cheddar; The Wrong Trousers, in which nefarious penguin Feathers McGraw employs a new Wallace patent in a daring heist; and A Close Shave, in which our heroes must step away from their window washing concern to foil a sheep rustling operation.

screenings.title: Poetry
screenings.description: Mija (Yun Jung-hee) has been tasked with raising her troubled teenaged grandson, Jong-wook, while her daughter, Jong-wook’s single mother, works in far-off Busan. When her capacity as a caregiver is threatened by a diagnosis of Alzheimer’s, Mija begins to study poetry composition at the local cultural center—first inspired by beauty in the natural world, then, when Jong-wook is mired in shameful scandal, inspired by new depths of disappointment and pain. Written specifically for Yun, a leading light of ’60s and ’70s South Korean cinema who gives an achingly vulnerable performance, Lee’s poignant, penetrating drama was awarded Best Screenplay at Cannes in 2010.

screenings.title: Ray Gunn in 70mm
screenings.description: In Metropia, a gigantic city in an alternate future as seen from 1939, private eye Raymond Gunn is drawn into a case involving aliens, murder, and a multimedia star named Venus Nova.

screenings.title: A Long Winter
screenings.description: In 1951, high in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, Mike’s world is thrown into uncertainty when his mother vanishes into the wilderness. Alongside his complicated father, and with their small mountain community rallying together against the unforgiving winter, Mike embarks on a search that leads him toward an unexpected journey of self-discovery, belonging and the quiet strength required to carry on.

screenings.title: The Royal Ballet: the Nutcracker (2026)
screenings.description: At a cosy Christmas party, young Clara meets the mysterious magician Drosselmeyer, who gives her a nutcracker doll. When the guests have departed and the house is asleep, Clara sneaks downstairs in search of the doll. Instead, she finds Drosselmeyer, who whisks her away on a journey into a whole world of enchantment: fantastical landscapes of flurried snow and glittering confection where toys come alive and the magic never stops. Peter Wright’s production of this festive family favourite sparkles to the wondrous swell of Tchaikovsky’s orchestral score, alongside the glow and grandeur of Julia Trevelyan Oman’s period designs.

screenings.title: Wild Boys of the Road
screenings.description: “By the time Eddie breaks down and cries, ‘I’m sick of being hungry and cold! I’m sick of freight trains!’ both the romantic notion of the train and the idle fantasies of boyhood have been demolished. Suffering is everywhere and there’s no one to blame for it. Though this was a Pre-Code film, its intended ending was still too bleak for producer Jack Warner. If the new ending feels off, it’s a credit to the mounting sense of desperation Wellman built with the rest of the film, where there are no easy answers.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: Desperately Seeking Susan with Susan Seidelman in person
screenings.description: Screening followed by a Q&A with Susan Seidelman and Rachel Syme Dir. Susan Seidelman. 1985, 104 mins. U.S. 4K DCP. With Rosanna Arquette, Madonna, Aidan Quinn. A desperate New Jersey housewife (Rosanna Arquette) is rescued from terminal boredom when a bump on the head and a case of amnesia cause her to be mistaken for a Lower East Side free spirit (played by Madonna). Riffing gleefully on Jacques Rivette’s Celine and Julie Go Boating, this screwball romp through the hipster bohemia of 1980s downtown Manhattan is effortlessly directed by Susan Seidelman—coming off her breakthrough low-budget NYC gem Smithereens—and boasts appearances by indie icons like John Turturro, Richard Edson, John Lurie, Richard Hell, Rockets Redglare, and more. The soundtrack rocks Madonna’s club anthem “Into the Groove” alongside Iggy Pop, Run-D.M.C., and classic Motown. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / free for MoMI members. screenings.title: Nayak (The Hero)
screenings.description: “Trains often spell escape for characters in Ray’s films; Pather Panchali’s image of children running through a field to chase a locomotive is one of his most poignant. Nayak reverses the situation somewhat. For fading movie star Arindam Mukherjee (played uncomfortably close to type by matinee idol Uttam Kumar), the train he boards to avoid a flurry of bad press ends up returning him, nightmarishly, to himself.” —Series curator Genevieve Yue

screenings.title: Daughters of the Dust
screenings.description: “This landmark film by pioneering director Julie Dash forever changed my thinking about the Great Migration, not to mention Gullah culture. Her key participation in Anthology—foregrounding the contributions of the remarkable Ann Lowe and Eartha Kitt—reveals Dash’s distinctive voice and ongoing commitment to centering the lives of Black women.”—Sylvia Yount, Lawrence A. Fleischman Curator in Charge of the American Wing, The Metropolitan Museum of ArtPresented in DCP 4K

screenings.title: Cinexpérimentaux: a Meeting with Abigail Child
Pinball (with director Naveen Chaubal in person)
screenings.description: With director Naveen Chaubal and producer Bryn Silverman in person Dir. Naveen Chaubal. 2026, 86 mins. U.S. DCP. In English, Arabic with English subtitles. In this tender coming of age portrait, Yosef, a spirited athlete in Louisville, Kentucky, contemplates his past as a displaced Iraqi refugee, his present as an immigrant trying to make sense of his kaleidoscopic identity, and his uncertain future. As Yosef reaches milestones of adulthood—high school graduation, his sister’s departure from the U.S.—long-buried questions come to the surface: where does he belong? Has he truly escaped from the shadow of war? What does it mean to build a future in a place shaped by the same forces that displaced his family? Is the life he is living truly his own—or simply the safest one available to him? In director Naveen Chaubal’s feature documentary debut, Yosef dives into the memories of his journey from Iraq to America and, like the steel ball ricocheting inside a machine, navigates shifting social, cultural, political, and financial pressures, trying to find stillness, purpose, and a place to land in an increasingly chaotic world. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance
screenings.description: With filmmaker Matías Piñeiro in person The screening will be preceded by a book signing with Piñeiro at 3:00 p.m. Dir. John Ford. 1962, 123 mins. U.S. 35mm. With James Stewart, John Wayne, Lee Marvin, Woody Strode. Who shot the vicious outlaw Liberty Valance? Was it the law-and-order senator (James Stewart), representing the new order, or the rugged gunman (John Wayne), representing the pioneer tradition? There are no easy answers in this twilight western that serves as John Ford’s profound summation and reevaluation of his earlier movies and features Wayne and Stewart in two of their greatest late-career roles. The film that coined the phrase “When the legend becomes fact, print the legend,” The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance is, per Richard Brody, the “greatest American political movie,” a truth-seeking frontier tale about the free press, vigilantism, and the myth of the American male. To celebrate the release of a new book on filmmaker Matías Piñeiro (Viola), The Originals is proud to present a 35mm print of John Ford’s The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance, a film that Piñeiro writes about. Published by Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema, From where do you start when drawing a flower? is composed of Piñeiro’s notebooks, sketches, photographs, writings, and merges his filmmaking practice with his cinephilia as well as his longstanding work as a film educator. Writes Piñeiro: “As flowers are a motif in the title of my book, I could not help but think about one of the most beautiful flowers in film history: the cactus flower in The Man Who Shot Liberty Valance by John Ford. The beauty of this flower may reside in its extraordinary power for evoking a certain feeling of irrecoverable loss, a scar we have to learn to live with. This flower will be screened in a beautiful 35mm black and white print, as it was meant to be. The lack of color does something to this flower—we can’t learn all about it; we cannot fully pick it. It escapes us just in front of our faces but remains glowing within us.” From where do you start when drawing a flower? (Fireflies Press and Batalha – Centro de cinema) Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

screenings.title: Leviathan
screenings.description: Setting out on the high seas of the North Atlantic aboard a Massachusetts-based commercial fishing trawler, Castaing-Taylor and Paravel produced one of the most mesmerizing, visually distinctive, and startlingly immediate documentaries of the 21st century, using the unique agility of their lightweight GoPro cameras to capture perspectives unlike anything theretofore seen in cinema, from gull-like views of the vessel to plunges into the slimy viscera of the day’s catch. “The density of aural and visual stimuli overwhelms—and liberates.”—Melissa Anderson, The Village Voice

screenings.title: Still Life + Train-Trains #2: A Bypass
screenings.description: A program of two formally adventurous trainspotting films from the Middle East. Stephan’s memory piece Train-Trains #2: Bypass follows the weed-choked rails of a former train line, an extension of the Orient Express that once linked Lebanon to Palestine, which lives on in the memories of those who reside near its long-abandoned stations; Saless’s Still Life, a key film of the early Iranian New Wave and winner of the Silver Bear at the 24th Berlin International Film Festival, observes the daily lives of a longtime crossing guard (Zadour Bonyadi) at a remote train station and his wife, whose well-worn routine will be upended by an unexpected development.

screenings.title: The Celebration
screenings.description: The opening salvo in Dogme 95’s all-out assault on cinematic artifice, revolutionary in its emancipated use of the Sony DCR-PC7 Handycam, Vinterberg’s scorched earth melodrama/farce takes place during a gathering of the extended Hansen clan at a family-run hotel to mark the 60th birthday of solid burgher patriarch Helge (Henning Moritzen)—an event that takes a turn for the chaotic when Helge’s eldest son, Christian (Ulrich Thomsen), accuses his father of molesting both himself and his recently deceased twin sister during a dinner table toast. Abrasive, volatile, savagely funny, and endlessly inventive, one can scarcely feel indifferent towards such a blood-on-the-walls affair as this.

screenings.title: Lady Killer
screenings.description: Grémillon was still in the employ of Berlin’s UFA Studios when he began shooting this adaptation of an André Boucler novel which stars Jean Gabin as a Don Juan of the French Foreign Legion who sets his sights on seducing Mireille Balin—and accidentally falls in love for real. The atmospheric work of cinematographer Günther Rittau (The Blue Angel) connects Grémillon’s film to the legacy of German expressionism, while the electric reunion of Pépé le Moko co-stars Gabin and Balin and the film’s pervasive air of tragic romantic fatalism show an affinity with French poetic realism. Distributor: Grasshopper Film

screenings.title: Last Cabaret
screenings.description: Focused on a family-run cabaret soon to be shuttered, Shusuke Kaneko’s (Summer Vacation 1999) elegiac Last Cabaret would be the penultimate film in Nikkatsu’s erotic line—a bittersweet requiem for the end of Roman Porno.

screenings.description: In 1951, high in Colorado’s Rocky Mountains, Mike’s world is thrown into uncertainty when his mother vanishes into the wilderness. Alongside his complicated father, and with their small mountain community rallying together against the unforgiving winter, Mike embarks on a search that leads him toward an unexpected journey of self-discovery, belonging and the quiet strength required to carry on.

screenings.title: Stalker
screenings.description: Tarkovsky’s stunning, haunted sepia-toned sci-fi masterpiece follows a scientist and a writer who, living in a broken-down totalitarian dystopia, recruit the help of a “Stalker”—a kind of post-apocalyptic Sherpa—to guide them on a voyage of self-discovery, passing through the bleak, otherworldly Zone in hopes of finding therein a haven that will fulfill their secret desires. An enigmatic, austere, and utterly immersive experience that combines religious allegory and political prophesy, and has kept cinephiles debating its meaning for some 50 years.

screenings.title: The Inugami Family
screenings.description: Based on Seishi Yokomizo’s 1951 bestseller The Inugami Curse, adapted before and after Ichikawa’s 1976 blockbuster, but arguably never bettered—mystery/melodrama The Inagami Family takes place in the fallout following the death of the wealthy patriarch of the eponymous clan, whose members start to drop off like flies in the most unnatural of ways, leaving detective Kosuke Kindaichi (Kōji Ishizaka, who would play the same role for Ichikawa in four more Kindaichi films) on a race to ferret out a culprit before the reading of the will. Simmering resentments, a veritable army of closeted skeletons, and more twists than a super-coaster make this a must-see for the whodunnit addict.

screenings.title: Afternoons of Solitude
screenings.description: Serra’s visceral yet elegant documentary portrait of young, Peruvian-born superstar torero Andrés Roca Rey sees him risking life and limb on the clock, and in unglamorous off-hours traveling via minibus between arenas with an extensive, officious entourage. A privileged, patiently observed perspective on the flamboyant showmanship, ritualized grace, and terrible violence of bullfighting, that most controversial of the sporting arts, its time-honored spectacle of man’s cultivated, calculated intelligence facing down an elemental force of primal animal aggression, a spectacle that ends, invariably, in a welter of hot, bubbling blood. “Impressionistic and intimate… Perhaps the most immersive encapsulation of tauromachy yet achieved in cinema.” —Sight & Sound

screenings.title: The Fence
screenings.description: A vast public works project in West Africa. Horn, the construction site manager, and Cal, a young engineer, share lodging behind the double gates of their compound. Leone, Horn’s recent bride, comes to join them the same night that a man appears at the fence. His name is Alboury. Like a specter in the darkness, he demands the body of his brother who died earlier that day on the site. He will hound the two men all night long until they return it, as Leone watches the disaster play out before her.

screenings.title: Keane
screenings.description: Kerrigan, whose debut Clean, Shaven was one of the most harrowingly immersive portrayals of schizophrenia ever put on screen, dove back into the depths of a turbulent, fractured mind with the equally-if-not-more accomplished Keane, in which Damian Lewis, playing a mentally unsound William Keane, wanders the dingy corridors of the Port Authority Bus Terminal and other sordid pockets of New York City. Haunted by the memory of his young daughter’s abduction, he eventually strikes up a relationship with a young mother and her child (Amy Ryan and Abigail Breslin). A work of brilliantly sustained discomfort and tactile seediness, raw, rigorous, and entirely riveting.

screenings.title: Rex: A Dinosaur's Story
screenings.description: Released just two weeks before Jurassic Park and famed for the off-camera exploits of its director, flamboyant media mogul Kadokawa, Rex: A Dinosaur’s Story managed to do a brisk business at the Japanese box office, tugging heartstrings in telling the story of Chie (Yumi Adachi), a paleontologist’s daughter who discovers a Tyrannosaurus egg with her father (Tsunehiko Watase) and then forms an unlikely friendship with the hatchling that emerges from within. Made with a lavish budget that allowed for contracting the services of special-effects world megastar Carlo Rambaldi (E.T., Possession, Lizard in a Woman’s Skin), Kadokawa’s charmingly bonkers, Christmas-set blockbuster has now been remastered, primed to meet a new generation of international fans.

screenings.title: Castration Movie ⅗ Year of the Hyaena + Q&A
screenings.description: Castration Movie is a multi-part postmodern epic by visionary auteur Louise Weard. ⅗ Year of the Hyaena contains part of one chapter. In Chapter iii. Chastity No Exit Virtue Cuck, Michaela (Louise Weard) tries to be a good person.

screenings.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey
screenings.description: Dir. Stanley Kubrick. 1968, 149 mins. U.S/U.K. 4K DCP. With Keir Dullea, Gary Lockwood. As brilliantly engineered as the space program itself, Stanley Kubrick’s mysterious and profound sci-fi epic—“the ultimate trip”—is about nothing less than the beauty and the banality of civilization, blending cool satire, an elaborate vision of the future, and passages of avant-garde cinematic inventiveness. Set in a future that is already the past, 2001: A Space Odyssey envisions space travel as both hilariously routine and mind-bending, a journey to the infinite and beyond that forever changed the way we see the universe and cinema itself. Kubrick’s surreal masterwork still has the ability to conduct viewers to untold, unknowable realms of artistry and daring. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / $7 MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. The cost of admission may be applied toward a same-day purchase of a membership. Order tickets. Please pick up tickets at the Museum’s admissions desk upon arrival. All seating is general admission.

Straight Circle
screenings.description: A pair of enemy soldiers stationed on a remote border in a vast featureless desert descend into a state of profound disorientation after forgetting which side of the border is which. As they grapple with their identities, loyalties, and the absurdity of their situation, their isolation slowly gives way to an unfathomable nightmare that will blur the line between friend and foe.

screenings.title: Rock 'n' Roll High School
screenings.description: Dir. Allan Arkush, Joe Dante. 1979. DCP. The Ramones, P.J. Soles, Dey Young, Vince Van Patten, Clint Howard, Mary Woronov, Paul Bartel. There’s only one thing that Riff Randal (P.J. Soles) cares about, and that’s The Ramones. When the villainous Principal Togar (Mary Woronov) goes on a campaign to outlaw the rock music and confiscates Riff’s concert tickets, her only chance to meet her punk rock idols, the rock ‘n’ roll rebel and her friends go toe-to-toe with the scholastic sadist in a fight for control of “Rock ‘n’ Roll High School.” This joyfully absurd, Roger Corman–produced celebration of youthful rebellion pounds with the heartbeat of punk rock’s most influential band. Tickets: $17.50 / $12 senior and students / $10 youth / free for MoMI members. There is a $1.50 transaction fee per ticket for all online purchases. screenings.title: Nocturama
screenings.description: Bonello’s ingeniously structured terror attack thriller opens with a group of tense, shifty teens prowling the streets and subways of Paris, in the midst, as it happens, of pulling off an intricately planned bombing plot. After the explosions, however, the film becomes something altogether different, as these pretty, vacant subversives tuck away inside a luxe department store and lose themselves in consumer culture—clothes, televisions, toys, and a stirring soundtrack that includes Blondie, Chief Keef, Shirley Bassey, Willow Smith, and Bonello’s menacing electronic score—all the while oblivious to the authorities tightening a net around them. A damning “allegory of nihilism and decadence” (Film Comment), fairly steeped in late Millennial malaise.

screenings.title: Scarface [35mm]
screenings.description: De Palma’s ultraviolent, ultra-quotable, ultra-colorful, ultra-everything remake of Howard Hawks’s gangster classic is the crass, visually loud flipside to the sober, muted The Godfather, a massively deranged and gleefully disreputable tale of the rise and plunging downfall of a Cuban immigrant turned Miami drug kingpin. Al Pacino throws himself into the title role with the fury of an angry Rottweiler, while Michelle Pfeiffer glowers gorgeously in her breakthrough role as his trophy wife. Featuring cinema’s second most shocking shower scene, a script by Oliver Stone, and a surging soundtrack by Giorgio Moroder, Scarface might just be the film of the Reagan ’80s.

screenings.title: The Matrix Revolutions
screenings.description: A digital downpour of Matrix code drenches the final showdown between Neo (Keanu Reeves) and Agent Smith (Hugo Weaving) in but one show-stopping moment in the third entry of the Wachowskis’ fin-de-millenium-defining series, which brings back Laurence Fishburne’s Morpheus, Carrie-Anne Moss’s Trinity, Jada Pinkett Smith’s Niobe, and other familiar-the-world-over faces for one more raucous round of raging against the machine. “An exercise in spectacular mayhem… There’s a hint of Burroughsian grandeur to [it’s] cyborg-against-cyborg ballet mécanique… BX cable squid spaghetti static electricity! Machine-gun machine-hell Armageddon!! Infernal orange and blue orgone-light tentacle vortex!!!” —J. Hoberman, The Village Voice
